items.finding: Presents a modular reference architecture and four-dimensional taxonomy of agentic AI systems, noting design trade-offs, recurring failure modes and evaluation methodologies including operational cost. Memory is not specifically highlighted in the abstract.
items.limitations: Broad survey; memory is not a focus; no systematic review method is stated in the abstract.

items.method: literature survey and taxonomy
items.finding: Proposes a seven-layer trust taxonomy (including memory and retrieval layers) and six secure-coordination design patterns for multi-agent LLM systems. Hallucinations can propagate across agent boundaries.
items.limitations: Focus on security and hallucination in multi-agent systems; memory is only one layer; no empirical evaluation.

items.method: system implementation with reported metrics
items.finding: A multi-agent email response system combining RAG over vector databases and ReAct agents with SQL toolkit reached 91.2% classification accuracy and an 88.4% end-to-end success rate.
items.limitations: Application paper; no memory ablation or comparison; RAG is used for knowledge retrieval rather than long-term agent memory.

items.method: benchmark construction and evaluation
items.sample: 143 multi-session tasks across 19 BIM projects and 4,016 prior sessions
items.finding: Introduces IFCMemoryBench to evaluate long-term memory when agents must combine remembered context from earlier sessions with live IFC queries. The framework decomposes memory performance into ingestion, retrieval and utilization.
items.limitations: Single domain (BIM); the abstract is truncated, so results on specific memory architectures are not visible; preprint.

items.method: paired counterfactual multi-agent rollouts
items.finding: Toxic content compressed into memory summaries can fall below toxicity detection thresholds yet still raise downstream toxicity. Raw transcript reuse drives overt toxicity while compressed memory carries hidden sub-threshold influence (measured by the sub-threshold propagation gap).
items.limitations: Concerns safety/toxicity rather than task success; simulated multi-agent setting; preprint.

items.method: unclear from abstract (system proposal evaluated on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S benchmarks with GPT-4.1-mini and Qwen3-8B; abstract truncated)
items.finding: LeanMem is a lightweight long-term memory framework that filters low-value content and stores it as profile, event, or record memory. It selectively updates only evolving event memories and adapts memory type and retrieval budget to each query, aiming to cut token use without losing fine-grained evidence. Quantitative results are cut off in the abstract.
items.limitations: Abstract is truncated, so results are not visible. The benchmarks are conversational memory (LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S) rather than multi-step task success. It is a preprint with no citations.

items.method: conceptual/theoretical article
items.finding: The paper argues that dynamic capabilities in firms require blending analytic and intuitive cognitive and emotional processes, drawing on social cognitive neuroscience. It does not address LLM agents.
items.limitations: Off-topic: strategic management; 'reflexion/reflection' is unrelated to LLM agent memory.

items.method: narrative review
items.finding: Reviews evidence on the relation between attention and memory across working memory, long-term memory, development and neuropsychology, organized by an embedded-processes view.
items.limitations: Human cognitive psychology; no LLM agents or task success measures.

items.method: laboratory conditioning experiments
items.sample: harnessed honeybees (n not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Honeybees learn side-specific associative mechanosensory conditioning of the proboscis extension reflex, with memory still present 24 h later and an optimal interstimulus interval around 4 s.
items.limitations: Off-topic: insect reflex conditioning; unrelated to LLM agents.

items.method: unclear from abstract
items.finding: The abstract contains only a licensing statement and no substantive content. The title suggests a history/memory framework for history education, unrelated to LLM agents.
items.limitations: No usable abstract; off-topic.

items.method: laboratory conditioning experiments
items.sample: harnessed honeybees (n not stated in abstract)
items.finding: Intact harnessed bees can learn visual discrimination via sting extension reflex conditioning with shock punishment, and antennae ablation impaired rather than helped learning.
items.limitations: Off-topic: insect learning; unrelated to LLM agents.

items.method: neurophysiological recordings in anesthetized animals
items.sample: 4 infant macaques
items.finding: NOT-DTN neurons in infant macaques are direction selective shortly after birth but have lower selectivity, truncated velocity tuning and weaker V1 input than adults.
items.limitations: Off-topic: primate visual neuroscience; very small sample.

items.method: narrative historical review and theory proposal
items.finding: Proposes a theory of autonomic socioemotional reflexes in mother-infant co-regulation after a narrative history of nervous system theories.
items.limitations: Off-topic theoretical paper on developmental psychology; no empirical test in the abstract.

items.method: modeling/methods comparison of pupil size equations
items.finding: Presents and compares models to calculate pupil size from luminance, age and other parameters so the pupillary light reflex can be decoupled from other influences.
items.limitations: Off-topic: pupillometry; memory is mentioned only as a possible pupil influence.

items.method: method proposal with benchmark experiments
items.sample: HotpotQA and ALFWorld with various backbone LLMs
items.finding: KnowAgent uses an action knowledge base and self-learning to constrain planning paths, achieving comparable or superior performance to baselines and reducing planning hallucination.
items.limitations: Knowledge base is explicit action knowledge rather than long-term experiential memory; abstract gives no numeric results or memory ablation.

items.method: method proposal with benchmark evaluation
items.sample: interactive instruction-following benchmark, seen and unseen environments
items.finding: CAPEAM combines context-aware planning with environment-aware memory of object states and locations, reaching state-of-the-art results with up to +10.70% gain in unseen environments.
items.limitations: Embodied household agent rather than a pure LLM agent; memory is task-episode environment state; abstract does not isolate the memory ablation.

items.method: single-system production deployment case study (90 days), no stated baseline beyond manual comparison
items.sample: One IT infrastructure management deployment (Proxmox, Kubernetes, networking, security) over 90 days
items.finding: Mind-Tool, which combines a persistent memory layer, a desired-state goal model and a reasoning engine, reported a 94% task success rate, 68% workflow automation and 62% time reduction versus manual approaches. The authors argue that domain memory design matters more than model intelligence.
items.limitations: Single deployment with no memory ablation, so the effect of memory cannot be isolated. The comparison is against manual work, not other agents. Self-reported results from the system's own authors, and the claim that it validates Anthropic's work is asserted, not tested.

items.method: narrative/systematic review with a mathematical formalization of CBR; no clear review protocol stated
items.finding: The paper reviews how Case-Based Reasoning (case retrieval, adaptation, learning) can be integrated into LLM agents to supply experience-based memory. It compares CBR-enhanced agents with Chain-of-Thought and standard RAG and discusses the role of self-reflection and other cognitive dimensions.
items.limitations: Abstract gives no review protocol, number of studies or quantitative success-rate results. Conceptual and theoretical focus, and the abstract is truncated.

consensus.statement: Adding an external experience memory (verbal reflections, induced workflows, graph memory, retained traces) raises success over no-memory or stateless baselines on sequential decision tasks, though the standalone gain can be modest.

On decision-task evidence only, task-structured memory beat unstructured alternatives: the AriGraph memory graph outperformed full history, summarization and retrieval augmentation in text games, and Agent Workflow Memory improved success on Mind2Web and WebArena while cutting steps on WebArena. The context-reduction mechanism is asserted rather than isolated, and the harness study below contradicts a general advantage.

On conversational and QA memory benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval, Long-MT-Bench+, not multi-step task success), memory unit granularity, graph-organized memory and iterative retrieval improve retrieval accuracy. The best structure is task-dependent, and mixed memory is the most resilient under noise.

Reflection or post-episode rule extraction that writes lessons back to memory improves later performance without weight updates. This rests on single-benchmark ablations and small-domain results, so confidence is moderate.

Unselective memory (excessive retrieval or unbounded writes) degrades precision or sequential-decision success. Direct cost, latency and error-propagation measurements for task success remain sparse and mostly self-reported.

Memory-specific benchmarks (MemoryAgentBench, MemoryArena, MemGym, IFCMemoryBench) were built because existing benchmarks do not isolate memory. They add multi-session or incremental formats and separate ingestion, retrieval and utilization, but their abstracts do not report results.

conflicts.claim: Whether structured memory gives a general advantage over simpler memory on sequential decision tasks

side_a.statement: Structured, task-built memory (AriGraph's memory graph, AWM's induced workflows) outperformed history, summarization and retrieval baselines, or improved success and step efficiency.

side_b.statement: In a controlled harness with three backbones and four suites, no single memory substrate dominated, and excessive retrieval harmed sequential decision-making, which contradicts a general structured-memory advantage.

conflicts.hypothesis_for_conflict: AriGraph and AWM are bespoke agents whose memory construction, update and use are co-designed for one environment family and compared against selected baselines. The harness holds substrates fixed across models and suites, so the gains may come from domain-tuned design rather than structure itself. Retrieval breadth and intensity may also differ across studies, and both sides are preprints with truncated or no-ablation abstracts.

conditional.statement: Under 75% distractor writes on ALFWorld, only the trace-aware TraceRetain policy preserved success (97/100), while plain bounded retention (FIFO) and unbounded memory degraded in precision. On clean ALFWorld the bounded policies were statistically indistinguishable, and this is a single-environment, two-seed result.

Low confidence: forgetting and pruning are reported to help (VIMBank's Ebbinghaus-style forgetting with 10-20% self-reported gains and ~23% lower reasoning cost, AdMem's reward-based pruning with no numbers), but this is self-reported and sits in tension with the null retention effect on clean ALFWorld.

In one ScienceWorld ablation (SwiftSage), self-reflection was the strongest standalone contributor and episodic memory helped most once the runtime loop was stabilized; this should not be generalized beyond that single benchmark and agent.

Broad retrieval helps long-context factual QA but can hurt sequential decision-making. Memory-conditioned planning (RAP, TRAD) is reported to work when retrieved content is step-relevant, but without ablation numbers or isolated memory effects.

synthesis.coverage_note: rq5 (benchmarks) is the best covered, though most benchmark abstracts lack results, and rq1 and rq2 have moderate evidence, much of it from conversational QA rather than multi-step tasks. rq4 (memory-planning interaction) is thin: only RAP (no numbers), TRAD (no results), the planning survey, JARVIS-1 and CAPEAM (no isolating ablation) address it, and no study ablates memory retrieval inside planning or decomposition loops. rq3 has few controlled ablations, with only ALFWorld and ScienceWorld single-environment studies. rq6 is thin: cost and latency claims are self-reported (VIMBank, MRAgent), error propagation is unmeasured for task success, and the toxicity paper is tangential. For rq1, no paper compares episodic, semantic and hierarchical memory head-to-head, and the duplicate JARVIS-1 and agent-survey entries should not be counted twice. The harness study 10.48550/arxiv.2608.15008 already covers multiple models and suites, so the remaining gaps are multiple seeds, variation of the agent loop, and full per-design results. A further gap is the dose-response threshold at which broader retrieval turns harmful, which that study reports only qualitatively. No new searches were possible here, so the rq1, rq3, rq4 and rq6 gaps flagged by the critic remain open.

gaps.description: No study compares episodic, semantic and hierarchical long-term memory head-to-head on multi-step task success while holding the agent loop fixed. The controlled harness reports that no substrate dominates, but its abstract shows no multiple seeds, no variation of the agent loop and no full per-design results. AriGraph and AWM each use bespoke, co-designed memory against selected baselines, so structure cannot be separated from domain tuning.
gaps.proposed_rq: Holding backbone and environment fixed, do episodic, semantic, hierarchical and graph memory differ in multi-step success, and does the ranking change with the agent loop (ReAct, Reflexion-style, plan-then-execute)?
gaps.method: Pre-registered factorial experiment: 4 memory designs x 3 agent loops x 3 backbones, with at least 5 seeds per cell and success rate as the main outcome, analysed with mixed-effects models. Re-implement AriGraph-style and AWM-style memory inside the common harness to test whether their gains survive without domain-specific co-design.
gaps.data: ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, WebArena and Mind2Web task splits with held-out evaluation tasks, using open-source harness code plus public benchmarks. Roughly 50-100 held-out tasks per suite.

gaps.description: The harness study reports only qualitatively that excessive retrieval harms sequential decision-making while broad retrieval helps long-context QA. The threshold at which retrieval turns harmful, and whether relevance quality shifts it, has not been measured. QA work finds iterative retrieval beats single-step retrieval, and step-level retrieval is claimed to reduce irrelevant context, but neither is tested as a dose-response effect on task success.
gaps.proposed_rq: How does task success change as the number or token budget of retrieved memory items increases, and does step-level versus trajectory-level retrieval move the point at which success starts to fall?
gaps.method: Within-agent dose-response experiment sweeping top-k (0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20) crossed with retrieval granularity (step vs trajectory) and oracle versus noisy relevance. Fit per-condition curves of success against retrieved tokens and estimate the inflection point with bootstrap CIs.
gaps.data: ALFWorld and WebArena with one memory store populated from earlier episodes, using 2-3 backbones and at least 3 seeds. Matched QA tasks (LongMemEval) serve as a contrast condition.

gaps.description: No study ablates memory retrieval inside planning or task-decomposition loops on long-horizon tasks. RAP, TRAD and CAPEAM link retrieved experience to planning, but their abstracts give no numbers or no isolating ablation. The planning survey treats memory only as one category of planning enhancement, so whether memory helps at plan time, at execution time, or both is unknown.
gaps.proposed_rq: Does giving the planner access to retrieved memory improve long-horizon success more than giving it only to the executor, and does plan reuse from memory add gains beyond step-level hints?
gaps.method: Controlled ablation of one plan-and-execute agent with memory access at planning only, execution only, both, or neither, plus a plan-reuse arm. The main outcome is success on tasks needing 10 or more dependent steps, with failures coded by whether the plan or the execution broke.
gaps.data: MemoryArena-style interdependent multi-session tasks and WebArena or ALFWorld long-horizon subsets. About 200 tasks, 3 seeds, and trace logs for failure coding.

gaps.description: Controlled evidence on consolidation, forgetting and pruning is nearly absent. Forgetting and reward-based pruning gains come from self-reported or number-free preprints, while the one controlled ALFWorld study finds bounded retention indistinguishable on clean tasks and benefits only under synthetic distractor noise with TraceRetain. Whether these mechanisms help under realistic, naturally accumulating noise across many sessions is untested.
gaps.proposed_rq: Across many sequential sessions with naturally accumulating, partly outdated entries, do Ebbinghaus-style forgetting, reward-based pruning and trace-aware retention improve success over FIFO and unbounded memory?
gaps.method: Longitudinal ablation over 20+ consecutive sessions comparing unbounded, FIFO, forgetting-curve, reward-pruning and TraceRetain policies, with success measured at fixed session checkpoints. Include a selective-forgetting probe in which earlier facts become invalid.
gaps.data: MemoryAgentBench's incremental formats and multi-session agentic tasks (MemoryArena, IFCMemoryBench), with at least 3 seeds and no synthetic noise injection.

gaps.description: Cost, latency and error propagation of long-term memory are not measured against task success. Cost and latency savings are self-reported, the harness study notes costly or brittle substrates without per-design numbers visible, and no study measures how a wrong stored memory affects later tasks. The only propagation evidence is a toxicity study in a simulated multi-agent setting, which does not address task success.
gaps.proposed_rq: How do erroneous or poisoned memory entries affect later multi-step success for different memory designs, and what is success per token and per second once memory costs are included?
gaps.method: Fault-injection experiment inserting 0%, 10% and 30% incorrect lessons or workflows into each memory design, measuring the drop in success and the number of later episodes affected. Report cost-adjusted success (success per 1k tokens and per minute) with and without memory.
gaps.data: ALFWorld and WebArena episodes with logged token and latency counts. Faults are generated by corrupting stored reflections or workflows, using 2 backbones and at least 3 seeds.

limitations: Only abstracts and metadata were read, not full texts, so numbers, ablation details and experimental controls could be missed or misread; several benchmark and method abstracts report no results at all.

Search covered OpenAlex and arXiv only within a limited time window, and 73 of 312 candidates were evaluated. Much of the evidence is preprints that are not peer reviewed, and some entries are duplicates (JARVIS-1, the agent survey) that should not be counted twice.

The sub-question on memory-planning interaction (rq4) is effectively unanswered: RAP, TRAD, CAPEAM, JARVIS-1 and the planning survey give no isolated memory ablation or success numbers. The critic's requested follow-up searches for rq1, rq2, rq3, rq4 and rq6 could not be run, so these gaps remain open.

Evidence on retrieval and storage mechanisms (rq2) comes mostly from conversational and QA benchmarks rather than multi-step task success, so conclusions about task success are weakly grounded. The controlled evidence on retention and distractor noise is a single ALFWorld environment with two seeds, and the SwiftSage ablation is one benchmark and one agent.

Cost, latency and forgetting or pruning gains (VIMBank, MRAgent, AdMem) are self-reported or lack numbers, and error propagation affecting task success is unmeasured. The only propagation evidence is a tangential toxicity study in a simulated multi-agent setting.

The 'unselective memory degrades success' claim is only directly supported by one harness study; the other cited works show precision loss or QA noise resilience, so confidence is low. The structured-versus-simple memory 'conflict' is likely a scope difference (bespoke co-designed agents versus fixed-substrate comparison), not a true contradiction.

AriGraph와 AWM은 특정 환경에 맞춰 공동 설계되어 선별된 기준선과 비교된 반면, 통제된 harness 연구는 어떤 substrate도 우세하지 않다고 보고하므로, 이득이 구조 자체보다 도메인 맞춤 설계에서 나왔을 가능성이 있습니다. 조건부 결과로, ALFWorld에서 75% 방해 쓰기가 있을 때 TraceRetain만 성공률(97/100)을 유지했지만, 깨끗한 환경에서는 유지 정책 간 차이가 없었고 단일 환경·2개 시드 결과입니다. 광범위한 검색은 장문 QA에는 도움이 되나 순차 의사결정에는 해로울 수 있습니다. 핵심 Gap은 (1) 에피소드·의미·계층 메모리를 에이전트 루프를 고정한 채 직접 비교한 연구의 부재와 (2) 메모리 검색을 계획·분해 루프 안에서 분리해 검증한 연구의 부재입니다. 비용·지연·오류 전파와 통합·망각 효과에 대한 통제된 근거도 거의 없습니다.
